passage: The school gates opened at 7:45, and Ishita's car always pulled up at 7:40, cool air still on her arms. Today she noticed Pranav coming through the side gate, shirt stuck to his back, shoes grey with dust. "Where do you live?" she asked at the water cooler. "Past the brick kiln. Four kilometres. I walk with my sister." "Every day? Why don't you take a bus?" Pranav shrugged. "No bus goes there." In class, Ishita kept looking at his dusty shoes. Four kilometres. She felt something prickly, a bit like being caught cheating, though she hadn't done anything. At lunch she asked Ms D'Costa, "Why doesn't the bus go to Pranav's side?" Ms D'Costa put down her tiffin. "That's a very good question, Ishita. Let's find out together."

qa.q: How far does Pranav walk to school?
qa.a: Four kilometres, from past the brick kiln.

qa.q: What was the prickly feeling Ishita had in class?
qa.a: It was a kind of guilt, "like being caught cheating", though she hadn't done anything wrong.

qa.q: Ishita chose to ask Ms D'Costa why the bus doesn't go there. Why is that a good next step?
qa.a: It turns her guilty feeling into curiosity about the reason, and an adult can help her understand it instead of her just feeling bad.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt being asked "Why don't you take a bus?"
qa.a: Pranav may have felt a bit awkward explaining, since the answer, no bus goes there, is something he can't change.

grounding: A child who arrives by car notices a classmate walks four kilometres to school, feels uneasy, and starts asking why.

passage: I'm Rukmini, Kamal's didi. Last week Kamal's friend Sonu came over to do homework, and I watched something change in my little brother. Sonu stared at Kamal's desk and lamp for a long time. "You have your own table?" At Sonu's house, he said, there's one room and the TV is always on, so he does sums on the steps outside. Kamal went quiet. After Sonu left, Kamal asked Amma, "Why does Sonu's house only have one room?" Amma tried to explain about rent and jobs. Then I teased, "See, you're lucky," and Kamal got cross. "I didn't do anything wrong!" He stomped off. But that night I saw him clearing half his desk and asking Amma if Sonu could come every Tuesday. I don't know exactly what he was feeling. Something big, for nine.

qa.q: Where does Sonu do his sums at home?
qa.a: On the steps outside, because the TV is always on in the one room.

qa.q: Why might Kamal have got cross when Rukmini said "you're lucky"?
qa.a: He seemed to feel accused, as if having a desk were his fault, so he defended himself: "I didn't do anything wrong!"

qa.q: What did Kamal choose to do that night, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He cleared half his desk and asked if Sonu could come every Tuesday, turning his discomfort into a way to share 🙂

qa.q: How might Sonu feel coming over on Tuesdays?
qa.a: Sonu might enjoy a quiet table for sums and feel welcome, as long as it's offered as friendship rather than pity.

grounding: An older sister watches her little brother notice his friend has no quiet place to study, ask why, get defensive, and then share.

passage:
Monday. Divyansh got 18 out of 20 in the maths test and grinned. Mohit got 17. "I go to tuition three days a week," Divyansh told him. "Don't you?" Mohit shook his head.
Thursday. Buying pencils at the market, Divyansh saw Mohit behind the counter of his father's tea stall, doing homework between customers, the book balanced on a crate. Mohit waved. Divyansh waved back, then felt oddly hot. "Well, I study hard too," he muttered to his mother, though nobody had said he didn't.
Next Monday. At dinner Divyansh asked, "Papa, why does Mohit have to work at the shop?" Papa thought for a while before answering. The next day Divyansh brought his old guidebooks to school and slid them onto Mohit's desk. "I finished these. Want them?"

qa.q: What score did Mohit get in the maths test?
qa.a: Mohit got 17.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh mutter "I study hard too" when nobody had said otherwise?
qa.a: Seeing Mohit working at the stall made him uncomfortable, maybe a little guilty, so he became defensive.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Divyansh, and what did he do with it?
qa.a: Asking Papa why Mohit has to work was the turning point; the next day he offered Mohit his old guidebooks.

qa.q: How might Mohit have taken Divyansh's question about tuition on Monday?
qa.a: Mohit may have felt a little small, since tuition isn't an option for him and his 17 came without it.

grounding: Over a week a child notices a classmate studies at his father's stall without tuition, feels defensive, asks why, and shares.

passage: Neelam, you asked why I keep an extra lamp by the door. Listen to your Charu Nani. When I was nine, the power went every evening in our town. Our house had a generator, so I did homework under a bright bulb. One night I walked to the shop with Papa and saw my friend Shabnam sitting under the streetlight by the post office, copying sums and squinting. Next day I asked Amma, "Why does Shabnam study outside?" Amma said their house had no generator. My face went hot. I even said, "It's not my fault!" though nobody had said it was. But after that I kept asking why. Some evenings Shabnam came over, and we shared my bulb.

qa.q: Where was Shabnam studying?
qa.a: Under the streetlight by the post office, copying sums.

qa.q: Why did Charu burst out with "It's not my fault!" when nobody had blamed anyone?
qa.a: Charu felt guilty and a bit defensive on seeing the difference, so the words came out as if pushing blame away.

qa.q: What choice did young Charu make after that hot-faced moment, and what did it change?
qa.a: Charu kept asking why and invited Shabnam over to share the bright bulb, turning an uncomfortable feeling into something useful.

qa.q: What might those evenings under the streetlight have been like for Shabnam?
qa.a: Shabnam was probably used to squinting and just getting the sums done; sharing the bulb may have felt kind, as long as it came as friendship and not pity.

grounding: A child notices that a friend studies under a streetlight while their own home has light, feels guilty and defensive, and starts to ask why.

passage: The rain came down so hard that the headmistress sent everyone home at noon. Kishore climbed into the yellow school van, dry under his raincoat. Through the steamy window he saw Dolma tie a plastic bag over her books and start up the steep path behind the school, alone. "Uncle, why doesn't the van go to Dolma's side?" "No road there, only steps. Forty minutes' walk." Forty minutes. Kishore got home in five. He felt strange, as if he'd taken something without asking. Next morning he asked Dolma, "Do you walk every day? Even in exams?" "Every day," she said, shrugging. "I learn my spellings on the steps." That night Kishore asked his mother why some roads just stop.

qa.q: How long is Dolma's walk home?
qa.a: Forty minutes' walk, up steps.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling after he got home dry?
qa.a: He felt strange and a little guilty, as if he'd taken something without asking, because his ride was so much easier than Dolma's walk.

qa.q: What did Kishore do with that uneasy feeling, and why was it a good choice?
qa.a: He asked questions, first Dolma and then his mother, instead of looking away, which is how he started to understand that some children begin further back.

qa.q: How might Dolma see the walk, compared with how Kishore sees it?
qa.a: For Dolma it is simply every day, and she even uses it to learn spellings, while to Kishore it suddenly looks long and unfair 🤔

grounding: A child driven home in the rain sees a classmate climb a long path alone and starts asking why their starting points are so different.

passage: Every morning Papa dropped Siddharth, ten, at the school gate in their car, the radio playing and the AC humming. On Tuesday it poured. From the back seat, Siddharth saw Sumit from his class trudging along the highway's edge, soaked, holding a plastic bag over his books. It was at least three kilometres from the colony Sumit lived in. Siddharth pressed his face to the window. At lunch Sumit's socks were still wet. That evening Siddharth asked, "Papa, why does Sumit have to walk so far and we don't?" Papa put down his phone. "His family doesn't have a car, beta, and there's no school bus from there." "That's not fair," Siddharth said. He felt a strange heaviness, like he'd done something wrong, though he hadn't. "Can we give him a lift when it rains?" Papa thought, then nodded.

qa.q: What did Sumit hold over his books?
qa.a: He held a plastic bag over his books.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he asked Papa about Sumit?
qa.a: Siddharth felt curious and a little guilty, a heaviness as if he'd done something wrong, though he hadn't.

qa.q: What could Siddharth and Papa do next?
qa.a: They could talk to Sumit's family about lifts on rainy days, and Siddharth could keep asking why things are unequal instead of looking away.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel sitting in wet socks at lunch?
qa.a: Sumit probably felt uncomfortable and tired, perhaps embarrassed, after walking so far in the rain.

grounding: A child who arrives by car notices a classmate walking far in the rain and begins asking why, feeling curious and a little guilty.

passage:
"Where do you do your homework?" Bhavna asked, swinging her legs on the school bench.
"On the stairs," said Vinita.
"The stairs?"
"Our room is one room. My brothers watch TV and Dadi prays. So I sit on the stairs outside."
"Isn't it noisy?"
"Neighbours go up and down. But the light is good."
Bhavna thought of her own room: a desk, a lamp, a shelf of books, a door that shut. "I have a desk," she said slowly.
"Lucky."
Bhavna felt her face get warm. "It's not my fault," she said, too fast.
"I didn't say it was."
They were quiet. Then Bhavna asked, "Why is it like that?"
Vinita shrugged. "Some people have more rooms."
"Do you want to do homework at my house on Saturday?"
Vinita smiled. "Okay."

qa.q: Where does Vinita do her homework?
qa.a: She does it on the stairs.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna say "It's not my fault" too fast?
qa.a: Bhavna felt guilty and a bit defensive after realising how different their homes were.

qa.q: What small step did Bhavna take, and why is it kind?
qa.a: Bhavna invited Vinita to do homework at Bhavna's house, sharing a quiet space instead of feeling guilty alone.

qa.q: How does Vinita seem to see the difference?
qa.a: Vinita seems matter-of-fact, saying "Some people have more rooms," without blaming Bhavna.

grounding: A child learns a friend studies on noisy stairs while the child has a desk, and starts to ask why, feeling guilty, curious and a little defensive.

passage: I was twelve when I first really noticed. I'd go to the corner shop at night for milk, and there was Abhinav, from my class, sitting on the step under the street lamp, doing his maths homework. Every night. I had my own room and a table lamp. One night I asked him why he didn't study at home. "Power cut in our lane," he said. "Again." I walked home feeling weird. I thought: I got ninety in maths and he got seventy-five, and everyone called me clever. But he was doing sums under a street lamp with mosquitoes biting. I felt guilty, then annoyed at feeling guilty, then just curious. Why was our lane always lit? Next week I asked my teacher. She explained about the old wiring in some areas. I'm Jomon, and that was the first time I wondered who gets what, and why.

qa.q: Where did Abhinav do his maths homework?
qa.a: He sat on the step under the street lamp.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel walking home that night?
qa.a: Jomon felt guilty, then annoyed at feeling guilty, then curious about why things were so unequal.

qa.q: What did Jomon do with the curiosity, and why was it useful?
qa.a: Jomon asked a teacher about it, which turned an uncomfortable feeling into understanding about unequal starting points.

qa.q: How might Abhinav see his nightly studying?
qa.a: Abhinav seems to accept it as normal, simply explaining the power cut, perhaps not expecting anyone to notice.

grounding: A child notices a classmate studying under a street lamp and starts asking why their starting points differ, feeling guilty and curious.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 5B
This week Hrithik asked me something I haven't forgotten. His father drops him at the gate by car every morning. On Monday, the car passed Divyansh walking on the highway road with his bag, a long way from school.
Hrithik came in and asked, "Ma'am, why does Divyansh walk so far? Why doesn't someone drive him?" Then, a bit sharply, "It's not my fault, is it?"
I told him it wasn't his fault, and that it was a good question. We talked about how families have different things.
On Thursday, Hrithik asked his father if they could give Divyansh a lift when they passed him. His father agreed.

qa.q: How does Hrithik get to school every morning?
qa.a: His father drops him at the gate by car.

qa.q: What does Hrithik's sharp question, "It's not my fault, is it?", suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he feels a little guilty and defensive, noticing for the first time that he has something Divyansh doesn't.

qa.q: How did the teacher's answer help Hrithik?
qa.a: By saying it wasn't his fault and that it was a good question, the teacher let him stay curious instead of guilty, which led to his idea of offering a lift.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel if Hrithik's family offers him a lift?
qa.a: Divyansh may feel grateful but also a little shy, depending on how kindly it is offered.

grounding: Shows a child noticing that a classmate walks far while he arrives by car, asking why, and feeling guilty and defensive at first.

passage:
Thursday
Today I went to Akash's house for the first time to do our science project. His whole family lives in one room. His little sisters were watching TV, his mother was cooking in the corner, and his grandfather was coughing.
I'm Bidisha. At home I have my own desk by the window, and nobody comes in when I study.
We tried to work on the floor, but his sister kept knocking the chart. Akash didn't complain. He just said, "I study at night when they sleep."
I felt strange on the walk home. Sort of guilty. Sort of confused. Why do I get a desk and he gets the floor?
Next time I'll ask if he wants to work at my house.

qa.q: When does Akash study?
qa.a: He studies at night when they sleep.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling on the walk home?
qa.a: Bidisha felt guilty and confused, noticing that Akash has no quiet place to study while Bidisha has a whole desk.

qa.q: What small step could Bidisha take next?
qa.a: Bidisha could invite Akash to work at Bidisha's house or at the school library, offering it as friends, not as charity.

qa.q: How might Akash feel about Bidisha seeing his home?
qa.a: Akash might feel a little self-conscious, but also relieved that Bidisha didn't make a fuss.

grounding: Shows a child noticing that a friend has no quiet place to study and starting to ask why, feeling guilty and curious.

passage:
Bhavna rode her new bicycle to the village school every morning. It took ten minutes. One day her chain broke, and she had to walk. On the way she caught up with Reena.
"How long do you walk every day?" Bhavna asked.
"An hour. After I fill water for the house and feed the goats."
Bhavna stared. She hadn't known. In class, Reena always looked tired, and Bhavna had thought she was lazy.
That evening, Bhavna asked her father, "Why do we have a bicycle and Reena doesn't?" He thought for a while before answering.
The next week, Bhavna started waiting for Reena at the crossroads so they could share the ride.

qa.q: How long does Reena walk every day?
qa.a: She walks an hour.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when she stared at Reena?
qa.a: She felt surprised and a little ashamed, realising she had thought Reena was lazy without knowing how hard her mornings were.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She started sharing the ride from the crossroads, a practical step once she understood Reena's longer journey.

qa.q: How might Reena feel about sharing Bhavna's bicycle?
qa.a: Reena may feel grateful and less tired, and glad someone understood her mornings.

grounding: Shows a village child discovering that a classmate walks an hour after chores while she rides, and starting to ask why.

passage: June in Johannesburg meant frost on the car windows. Bao's mum drove him to school every morning with the heater on. One Tuesday, at a red light, Bao saw Lindiwe from his class walking along the road, her breath making clouds, her hands pulled into her sleeves. The school was still far. "Mum, why does Lindiwe walk?" "Her family doesn't have a car, love." "But it's so cold." "Yes." Bao pressed his hand against the warm vent and suddenly didn't like how warm it was. At school, Lindiwe arrived late, rubbing her fingers. Bao wanted to say sorry, but for what? That evening he asked, "Could we give her a lift?" His mum thought. "We could ask her family."

qa.q: What did Bao see on the car windows in June?
qa.a: Frost.

qa.q: What was Bao feeling when he pressed his hand against the warm vent?
qa.a: He felt guilty and uneasy, suddenly noticing his warmth while Lindiwe walked in the cold, and curious about why things were different.

qa.q: What is a respectful next step for Bao's idea of a lift?
qa.a: Asking Lindiwe's family first, as his mum suggested, so the offer respects them instead of assuming.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe feel arriving late and cold every day?
qa.a: She may feel tired and uncomfortable, and perhaps embarrassed to arrive late for reasons that aren't her fault.

grounding: Illustrates a child noticing a classmate walks far in the cold while he arrives by car, and starting to ask why.

passage: During the Diwali holidays, the school ran a study camp in the library. Urmila noticed that Vandana always came first and left last, even though the camp ended at five. "Why don't you go home to study?" Urmila asked one afternoon. Vandana shrugged. "Our house is one room. My cousins are visiting for Diwali. There's nowhere to sit." Urmila thought of her own desk, the lamp, the closed door. "Oh." A boy nearby said, "Urmila's got her own room, lucky." "It's not my fault," Urmila snapped, surprising herself. Later she felt bad about it. On the way out she asked the librarian, "Can the library stay open longer for people who need it?" The librarian said she would ask the principal.

qa.q: How many rooms is Vandana's house?
qa.a: One room.

qa.q: Why did Urmila snap "It's not my fault"?
qa.a: She felt defensive and a little guilty when the boy pointed out her own room, as if she were being blamed for her advantage.

qa.q: What was helpful about Urmila's question to the librarian?
qa.a: It turned her discomfort into something useful: asking for more quiet study time for students who need it.

qa.q: How might Vandana see Urmila's questions?
qa.a: Vandana may feel a bit exposed explaining her home, but also noticed and perhaps glad someone asked the librarian.

grounding: Shows a child realising a classmate has no quiet place to study, asking why and feeling defensive and guilty.

passage: Before: In the week before Christmas, the class had online homework on a tablet app. Keerthana finished hers on her own tablet by seven. Elizabeth's answers always arrived after ten at night. During: The next Monday, Keerthana asked her, "Why do you do homework so late?" "We have one phone. Amma uses it for work till nine." Keerthana felt her cheeks warm. She had a tablet just for herself. She wondered why some people had more and some less, and whether that was fair. After: Three days later, she asked Miss, "Could we get extra time for people who share a phone?" Miss said yes, and quietly changed the deadline to the next morning for everyone.

qa.q: What time did Elizabeth's answers usually arrive?
qa.a: After ten at night.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when her cheeks felt warm?
qa.a: She felt guilty and a little embarrassed at having her own tablet, and curious about why things were so unequal.

qa.q: Why was Miss's change a thoughtful one?
qa.a: She moved the deadline for everyone, which helped Elizabeth without singling her out.

qa.q: What is it like for Elizabeth to wait for the family phone?
qa.a: She has to stay up late to finish work, and may feel tired and behind through no fault of her own.

grounding: Illustrates a child noticing a classmate lacks her own device, asking why and feeling guilty and curious.

passage: Swati, you asked why I always give the Kamble girls a lift in the rain. Let me tell you. When your Madhuri Nani was ten, in Nashik, our driver took me to school in a white car, even in the worst monsoon. One morning, splashing along the river road, I saw my classmate Sunanda walking, her schoolbag on her head, her skirt soaked to the knees. She walked five kilometres every day. I had never once thought about it. That night I asked my father, "Why does she walk and I don't?" He said, "Some people are luckier, that's all." I felt guilty, then cross, as if it were my fault. The next week I asked if Sunanda could ride with me. My father went quiet. Then he said yes.

qa.q: How far did Sunanda walk to school every day?
qa.a: Five kilometres.

qa.q: How did young Madhuri feel after her father's answer?
qa.a: She felt guilty and then cross, as if the difference were her own fault, and kept wondering why it was so.

qa.q: What choice in the story turned Madhuri's question into action?
qa.a: Asking her father if Sunanda could ride with her in the car, which shared a little of her head start.

qa.q: What might the car ride have meant to Sunanda?
qa.a: It probably meant a dry, less tiring start to the day, though she may also have felt shy accepting a lift from a richer classmate.

grounding: A child who rides to school by car notices a classmate walking far in the rain, asks why and feels guilty and defensive.
